explainer_reply:
The marked tokens span a wide variety of contexts and genres (fiction, news, dialogue, Q&A, even Russian text) with consistently low activation values. The tokens themselves share no coherent semantic theme — they are almost all extremely high-frequency items: function words (the, of, to, and, with, when, while, is, was, his, very, every), punctuation (periods, commas, quotation marks, slashes), and sentence/clause-boundary markers (Did, Meanwhile, As, The). Even the sub-word fragments (Re, ia, s, woman) occur in common words or names. The unifying pattern is token frequency rather than meaning: this neuron responds weakly and diffusely to common, predictable tokens in running text, with a slight tendency to fire at clause and sentence boundaries.

[EXPLANATION]: Weak, diffuse activation on high-frequency function words, punctuation, and clause/sentence-boundary markers across diverse texts — a common-token response with no specific semantic pattern.
